transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-09
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (Aurelia CTO), Marcus Lee (ML Eng Manager), Sofia Chen (Senior Engineer)
Shared links: Console demo deck (short): https://redwood.example/console-demo, Benchmark sheet: https://tiny.redwood/bench-aur123

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check on audio, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Dana (Aurelia): Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Alex: Great, I'm Alex, AE here at Redwood. Priya our solutions engineer will do most of the live demo. High level goal: show hosted API streaming behaviors, typical param choices, how we do retries and idempotency so your billing and UX are stable.
[00:22] Priya (Redwood): Hi all, excited — I'll toggle between the API and Console. We'll start with a short write-up of constraints and then run a few prompts from your sample set Marcus shared earlier. If anything is too deep feel free to pause.
[00:35] Marcus (Aurelia): Sounds good, mostly want to understand failure modes. We have interactive clinical triage chat so latency matters, also PII retention is a big red flag for us.
[00:46] Priya: Totally. On retention we keep request/response logs configurable — hosted default is 30 days but enterprise can request longer/shorter or disable retention, and we support KMS integration for keys. We'll share security whitepaper after.
[00:58] Dana: Is that the same thing as a private deployment? We aren't ready for full on-prem yet but need deterministic retention and audit.
[01:05] Alex: Good question, hosted can meet many compliance requirements with KMS + SOC2 attestation and VPC peering for network controls. Private is available if you need air-gapped ops — we can discuss later. For the demo Priya will show hosted flows.

[01:22] Priya: Ok starting the Console — I'm in the sandbox. First piece: streaming. By default our chat endpoint streams token deltas over SSE/HTTP2. For interactive apps you'll want low chunk sizes and tune "response.fragment_size" — sorry that's an internal name, in API it's handled by the stream rate and max_tokens.
[01:40] Sofia (Aurelia): In practice we see partial chunks come in ~150ms then a pause, can we tune that?
[01:46] Priya: Yes you can adjust generation params. Two quick knobs: temperature/top_p for creativity and max_tokens for length. On streaming there's also an effective latency knob: set beam-like constraints or lower max_tokens per chunk — but two tradeoffs: smaller chunks increase number of network packets and can slightly raise e2e cost.
[02:05] Alex: Also note the network path matters — if you use our closest region vs remote, you'll see a 30-60ms difference typical.

[02:18] Priya: Let's demo three prompts. First a short triage question (we'll run with temp=0.2, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=150). I'm going to hit the chat generate endpoint with streaming and an idempotency key.
[02:33] [API call shown briefly] Priya: Streaming begins, you can see tokens arrive incrementally. There's some small word corrections mid-stream — that's normal because the model is refining as it decodes.
[02:44] Marcus: If the stream drops mid-response what happens?
[02:47] Priya: Two things: client-side should resume or re-issue the call with the same idempotency key. On server we persist the generation state for a short time for exact resume on the same request if within N seconds (configurable). If not, we offer deterministic retry behavior by re-running with the same key and a fixed random seed for reproducibility — note: deterministic replay is best-effort and exact token alignment can vary across model variants.
[03:14] Dana: Hmm seed — does that add cost or latency?
[03:17] Priya: Slightly. Replay may re-run entire generation so cost can double in rare cases if you retry too frequently — that's why we recommend exponential backoff and a cap on retries.

[03:30] Alex: We recommend a client pattern: on stream disconnect do exp backoff start 250ms, then 500ms, 1s, after 3 attempts fall back to a shorter model or cached response. Also pass idempotency key so billing and content reconciliation stay stable.
[03:48] Sofia: For billing we need to ensure not double-charging if client re-sends — idempotency key solves that?
[03:53] Priya: Yes, if you use the same idempotency key the backend will dedupe within the time window. We'll surface a dedup flag in the response header when a replay was caught.

[04:05] Priya: Now I'll change params to higher temperature 0.8 and show differences — you'll see more divergent streaming outputs and sometimes longer pauses when the model explores less-likely tokens. That can affect perceived latency.
[04:20] Marcus: So for clinical triage do you recommend lower temp?
[04:23] Priya: Yes, lower temp (0.0-0.3) plus slightly higher top_p ~0.9 keeps answers conservative. We also use safety/rerank hooks in the pipeline for PII masking if you enable redact mode.

[04:36] [06:00] Priya: Switching to Console Optimize recommendations — Optimize analyzes your workload (prompt lengths, token distributions, latency SLOs) and proposes batching, cache, and quantization profiles. For interactive apps it typically suggests: prefix KV caching for repeated patient prompt contexts, batch size 1 with concurrency tuning, and quantized model variant for non-critical paths.
[06:20] Alex: A note on KV cache: it's most helpful when you have repeated context across requests, like a persistent patient history. It reduces per-token compute and can dramatically cut cost. It's not magic for single-shot questions.

[06:35] Marcus: Can we control how long KV cache entries live? We can't keep PHI in cache for long.
[06:40] Priya: Yes TTL is configurable per-tenant and you can choose encrypted cache storage. We log KMS key usage in audit logs.

[07:00] Dana: Ok about fallbacks — what's the simplest fallback path if hosted hiccups during peak?
[07:05] Priya: Two-tier fallback: 1) fall back to a smaller hosted model (lower GPU cost, faster) and 2) as a last resort use a cached templated response or degrade UI to search results. We demoed model routing earlier in another call; but in Console you can set routing policies by latency vs cost and put thresholds for automatic fallback.
[07:28] Alex: Also we have burst capacity options to handle sudden spikes if you prefer less functional fallback and more capacity.

[07:40] [08:15] Priya: I'm going to intentionally throttle the stream to emulate packet loss. Watch the client behavior: we've got fine-grained error codes for stream partials and finalization. The recommended client strategy is: treat transient stream closures as retryable, but treat 4xx style model errors as non-retryable.
[08:40] Sofia: What about idempotency scope — is it per conversation or per message?
[08:45] Priya: Per-request idempotency key. For conversation-level idempotency you can synthesize a key from conversation_id + message_hash.

[09:00] Marcus: Our platform is multi-tenant; can Redwood guarantee isolation on hosted?
[09:06] Alex: Yes, tenants are logically isolated. For stricter isolation we offer Dedicated pools where you get reserved GPUs and stronger network isolation. Hosted default is multi-tenant but still SOC2 and encrypted paths.

[09:25] Priya: Back to params — we also recommend setting "max_output_tokens" conservatively and applying a hard application timeout to stop streaming if it goes beyond SLO. That avoids runaway bills. In Console we show token-level cost projections per route.

[09:45] Dana: Ok what's the typical unit cost delta between streaming with high chunk frequency vs low frequency?
[09:50] Alex: It depends on model and seq length distribution. Roughly, more frequent small chunks can increase request overhead ~5-15% but reduce tail latency. Optimize will simulate your sample set and give an estimated delta.

[10:10] Priya: Now quick demo of retries: I will call the same request three times with the same idempotency key and intentionally fail one. Backend will dedupe and return the same content and mark header X-Redwood-Dedupe: true.
[10:28] [API call shown] Priya: See header presence in the response. If you reissue with a different key you'll be billed for a separate run.

[10:38] Marcus: Will dedupe cover partial streaming where some tokens were delivered then a reconnect?
[10:43] Priya: If you reconnect with identical key within the resume window we will attempt resume; if resumed, we deliver the remainder. If the resume window expired, dedupe still prevents double full runs within a short window, but partial deliveries might differ.

[11:00] Alex: For robust client-side code, our SDK has helpers for streaming reconnection and idempotency key generation. We'll share the sample client implementation.

[11:12] Dana: We need to align on security docs and also ask legal about data residency. Is that something you can provide?
[11:18] Alex: Yes, will send security whitepaper and SOC2 report. Also show KMS integration patterns in the docs.

[11:26] Priya: One more thing — for debugging we provide token-level tracing you can enable in a sandbox; this helps pinpoint where decoding differences occur but should not be enabled with PHI in production.

[11:40] Sofia: If we test a pilot, what's the typical pilot size and duration?
[11:44] Alex: Usually 4-6 weeks with up to 100k tokens/day to validate latency and quality. For enterprise we set an initial committed capacity if needed.

[12:00] Priya: Let's discuss the planned benchmark: we'll run three model variants (standard, quantized, small) against your prompt set. We'll measure p50/p95 latency and token cost. Marcus, can you drop the sample set in the bench sheet?
[12:11] Marcus: Yes I'll upload the sample prompts by Friday.

[12:18] [12:50] Alex: Quick recap and next steps: we'll send pricing + quickstart + security docs, Priya runs benchmark, customer shares prompts and completes security review, then schedule pilot kickoff. Any last q's?
[13:02] Dana: One minor — does Redwood support SAML SSO for the Console?
[13:06] Alex: Yes SAML and OIDC both supported. We'll include the SSO guide link.

[13:15] Marcus: Thanks that's helpful.
[13:18] Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the materials and proposed pilot plan.
[13:22] Dana: Thanks team, bye.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had minor speaker attribution errors and some technical terms came through a bit off (quan- tization, K V cash) — reviewed by AE for clarity.
